text: Your slides are finished. Then someone asks, what evidence supports that claim? Defend It helps you practise those questions before your presentation.
I load the Campus Cup sample, then select its boldest claim: an eighty percent reduction in campus cup waste. That's a prediction, not evidence.
The coach asks how a short pilot, limited budget, and no wider behavior data support that prediction. The question connects directly to the presentation.
My first answer leans on eighteen interested classmates. It sounds confident, but interest alone doesn't show that people will return cups.
The feedback recognizes the survey, then flags its narrow sample and missing validation. It suggests expanding the sample and looking for comparable programs.
I revise the same answer. Eighty percent becomes an untested goal. I acknowledge the limited sample, propose measuring actual returns, and include staff labor.
The recorded comparison calls the reasoning stronger. But the follow-up asks for metrics I already named. That's a real limitation, retained here rather than hidden.
Three prompt patterns support the workflow: a rigorous, kind coaching persona; few-shot examples demonstrating grounded feedback; and iterative refinement comparing two attempts on the same question.
Download the prep sheet to revisit your question, answers, and feedback. The coach can still miss things, so check its advice, then rehearse aloud.
